- When sentiment is strongly positive (≥0.6) and forecast is rising sharply, reduce peak forecasts by 5–10% to avoid overshoot.  
- If sentiment is negative (≤0.2) and forecast is falling, avoid underestimating the dip — add 2–5% buffer to prevent premature bottoming.  
- After a recent spike in price, model tends to overreact — cap 3–5 day forecasts at 10% below peak to reflect mean reversion.  
- If sentiment is volatile (alternating ±0.3) and forecast shows erratic swings, smooth transitions by averaging 2–3 prior values before projecting next.  
- For 30-day horizon, if true outcome deviates >10% from 14-day moving average, adjust forecast to align with recent 7-day trend, not 30-day trend.  
- When sentiment is low (≤0.3) and price is falling, model often underpredicts — add 3–5% to forecast to account for lingering downward momentum.  
- If sentiment is high (≥0.7) and price is rising, model often overestimates — reduce forecast by 5–8% to reflect sentiment cooling.  
- Always check if forecast is >15% above recent 14-day high — if so, reduce by 5–10% unless sentiment is strongly bullish.  
- If sentiment is neutral (0.3–0.6) and forecast is flat, avoid overfitting — use 14-day moving average as baseline, not 30-day.  
- For 30-day forecasts, if true outcome is below 10% of 30-day average, model often underestimates — add 2–5% to forecast to avoid premature bottom.
